entire_current.source_text: Example. $A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$: $(2-\lambda)^2-1=0$ gives $\lambda_1=3$, $\lambda_2=1$, $q_1=(1,1)/\sqrt2$, $q_2=(1,-1)/\sqrt2$, and $3q_1q_1^\top+q_2q_2^\top=\tfrac32\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}+\tfrac12\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1\\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=A$. In words: a symmetric matrix is a pure stretch along perpendicular axes (here by $3$ along the diagonal, by $1$ across it), with no rotation or shear.

entire_current.source_text:
Theorem — Rayleigh quotient
    
      For $A\in\mathbb S^n$: $\ \lambda_{\max}(A)=\max_{\|x\|=1}x^\top Ax$, $\ \lambda_{\min}(A)=\min_{\|x\|=1}x^\top Ax$, and $\lambda_{\min}\|x\|^2\le x^\top Ax\le\lambda_{\max}\|x\|^2$ for all $x$, with equality at the corresponding eigenvectors.
